questions.q: How does the summary describe our capacity for happiness?
a: An evolved trait that helped our ancestors survive
A learned habit shaped mainly by culture
A fixed personality feature we are born with
A modern invention created by consumerism
questions.why: Lesson 1 says happiness developed recently in human history and works as an adaptive survival trait.

questions.q: Which part of the brain lit up during happiness in the EEG scans?
a: The left side of the prefrontal cortex
The right side of the prefrontal cortex
The amygdala deep in the center
The cerebellum at the back of the brain
questions.why: Lesson 1 reports that activity in the left prefrontal cortex, a newer brain area, accompanied happy states.

questions.q: Once basic needs are covered, what does the summary say more money tends to do?
a: Reduce happiness by fueling comparison with others
Keep raising happiness at a steady rate
Leave happiness completely unchanged
Improve happiness mainly through better health
questions.why: Lesson 2 says extra income beyond a threshold stops helping and can hurt because we compare ourselves with neighbors.

questions.q: Why does the summary argue that progressive taxes could raise a country's happiness?
a: They weaken status competition and the chase for raises
They give governments more money for public services
They encourage people to work longer hours
They make housing cheaper for lower earners
questions.why: Lesson 3 says progressive taxation makes chasing the next raise less attractive and reduces comparison with others.

questions.q: Which country does the summary name as measuring Gross National Happiness instead of GDP?
a: Bhutan
Denmark
Costa Rica
New Zealand
questions.why: Lesson 3 notes that Bhutan is the only country that uses Gross National Happiness as its main statistic.
